q: What is a token, and what does a tokeniser do?
plain: A token is a small chunk of text that the model reads as one unit. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, or a single byte (one basic unit of computer data). Each token has an id number, which is its place in a fixed list called the vocabulary. A tokeniser turns a string of text into a list of id numbers (encoding), and back again (decoding). For example, GPT-2 (generative pre trained transformer, version 2) splits "Hello world" into two tokens. In that split, the tokens are "Hello" and " world", and the second one keeps its leading space. The tokeniser is trained separately before the model and then frozen (never changed again), so the model only sees integers (whole numbers).
deep: A tokeniser is a separate stage of the LLM pipeline with its own training set and algorithm (usually BPE). After training it implements two functions: `encode(str) -> list[int]` and `decode(list[int]) -> str`, and decode(encode(s)) should return s exactly. The vocabulary also holds **special tokens** such as `<|endoftext|>` that mark document boundaries or chat roles. The CME295 cheatsheet lists `[UNK]` for unknown text and `[PAD]` for filling sequences to equal length; byte level tokenisers never need `[UNK]`. Karpathy's tokenizer lecture argues many odd LLM behaviours trace back to this stage.
say: A token is the unit the model actually reads: a piece of text, often a word or part of a word, with an integer id in a fixed vocabulary. The tokeniser is the component that maps strings to lists of ids and back. The important thing is that it's trained separately, before the model, on its own data, and then frozen. So the model never sees characters, only those ids, which explains a lot of odd behaviour later, like trouble spelling words. For GPT-2 the vocabulary is about fifty thousand tokens.
must_mention: chunk of text with an id
encode string to ids, decode back

followups.q: Does the model ever see characters?
followups.a: No, only token ids; any character level knowledge has to be learned from the tokens.

traps: Saying the tokeniser is learned jointly with the model.

q: Why do LLMs use subword tokenisation instead of whole words or characters?
plain: Subword tokens avoid the problems of both whole words and single characters. A whole word vocabulary (the list of all tokens) becomes enormous, because every form of every word needs its own entry. A whole word vocabulary also fails on new words it has never seen. Characters never fail on new words, but they make sequences several times longer. Each character also carries very little meaning on its own. Subwords are the compromise: common words stay whole, and rare words split into pieces the model has seen before. For example, "unbelievably" might become "un", "believ" and "ably", and each piece is reused in many other words.
deep:
| Unit | Vocabulary | Sequence length | Unknown words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Word | Huge, every inflection | Short | Yes, `[UNK]` |
| Character or byte | 256 bytes | Very long | None |
| Subword | 30K to 200K | Medium | None with byte fallback |

Length matters because attention costs $O(T^2)$ and the context window is fixed in tokens (CME295 cheatsheet compares the three). Subwords share statistics across related forms, which a word vocabulary cannot. The cost: splits are statistical, not morphological.
say: It's a compromise between two bad extremes. A word vocabulary would need an entry for every inflection and still couldn't handle a word it hasn't seen, so you'd get unknown tokens. Characters or bytes never fail, but sequences get several times longer, and since attention cost grows with the square of length and the context window is counted in tokens, that's expensive. Subwords keep frequent words as single tokens and break rare words into pieces the model already knows. The trade off is that the pieces are statistical rather than linguistic, which is why spelling and digit arithmetic are hard.
must_mention: word vocabularies explode and have unknown words
attention cost grows with length squared
rare words split into known pieces

followups.q: What vocabulary sizes are typical?
followups.a: About 32K (Llama 2, Mistral) up to 128K (Llama 3) and around 150K (Qwen).

traps: Claiming subwords are chosen to match morphemes.

q: How is a BPE vocabulary trained? Work through a small example.
plain: Byte pair encoding (BPE) builds its vocabulary (the list of all tokens) by repeatedly gluing together the pair of neighbouring tokens that appears most often. BPE starts with the 256 possible bytes (the basic units of computer data) as its tokens. Then BPE counts every pair of neighbouring tokens in the training text. BPE merges the most frequent pair into one new token and repeats until the vocabulary reaches the size you asked for. On the 11 byte text "aaabdaaabac", the first merge joins "a a" into a new token. Three merges in total shrink those 11 bytes to 5 tokens. GPT-2 (generative pre trained transformer, version 2) did 50,000 merges, giving 50,257 tokens. The total is the 256 bytes, the 50,000 merges, and one special token (a reserved token that marks a document boundary).
deep:
Algorithm: ids = UTF-8 bytes; repeat: count adjacent pairs, take the most frequent, mint id $256 + k$, replace every occurrence, record the merge. Vocabulary size = base + merges.

```python
from collections import Counter
def merge(ids, pair, new_id):
    out, i = [], 0
    while i < len(ids):
        if i < len(ids) - 1 and (ids[i], ids[i + 1]) == pair:
            out.append(new_id); i += 2
        else:
            out.append(ids[i]); i += 1
    return out
ids = list("aaabdaaabac".encode("utf-8"))
for k in range(3):
    stats = Counter(zip(ids, ids[1:]))
    ids = merge(ids, max(stats, key=stats.get), 256 + k)
print(ids)   # [258, 100, 258, 97, 99], as in the minbpe README
```

GPT-2: 256 bytes + 50,000 merges + `<|endoftext|>` = 50,257 (Hugging Face tokenizer docs).
say: BPE is greedy compression. I start with the 256 byte values as tokens and convert the training text to bytes. Then I count every adjacent pair, take the most frequent one, give it a new id, replace all its occurrences, and record that merge rule. I repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size, so vocabulary size is 256 plus the number of merges. On a toy string like a a a b d a a a b a c, three merges compress eleven bytes into five tokens. GPT-2 ran fifty thousand merges.

followups.q: What is the time cost of naive BPE training?
followups.a: Each merge rescans the corpus, so it is merges times corpus length; real implementations update pair counts incrementally.

traps: Saying BPE starts from words.

q: Once a BPE tokeniser is trained, how does it encode new text?
plain: To encode new text, byte pair encoding (BPE) replays the merges it learned during training, in the order it learned them. First BPE converts the text to bytes. Then BPE applies the earliest learned merge that fits, then the next earliest, until no learned merge applies. BPE does not look at which pairs are common in the new text. For example, suppose "a a" was merge number 1 and "aa b" was merge number 3. Then encoding "aab" first makes "aa" and afterwards makes "aab". Decoding (turning id numbers back into text) looks up the bytes for each id number and joins them together. Finally the decoder reads the joined bytes as UTF-8 (8 bit Unicode Transformation Format, a standard way to store text as bytes).
deep: minbpe's `encode`: compute the pairs present, pick the one with the lowest merge index (`min(stats, key=lambda p: merges.get(p, inf))`), stop if it is not in the merge table, else merge and repeat. This reproduces training time segmentation deterministically. In regex based tokenisers this runs separately within each pre split chunk. Decoding concatenates byte strings; partial UTF-8 sequences decode with replacement characters (`errors="replace"`), which is why a model can emit invalid bytes mid character.
say: Encoding replays the merges. I convert the string to bytes, look at all adjacent pairs, and apply whichever pair has the lowest merge index, meaning the one learned earliest. I keep doing that until no pair in the sequence is in the merge table. It's deterministic and it ignores frequencies in the new text entirely, which surprises people. Decoding is the easy direction: look up each id's byte string, concatenate, and decode as UTF-8, with a replacement character if the model produced an incomplete multibyte sequence.
must_mention: stop when no learned merge applies

followups.q: Why can decoding fail?
followups.a: A token sequence can end mid character, so the bytes are not valid UTF-8; tokenisers decode with replacement.

traps: Saying encoding picks the most frequent pair in the new text.

q: Why do GPT tokenisers work on bytes and split text with a regex before merging?
plain: Bytes guarantee that any text can be encoded, and the regex splitting keeps the learned tokens sensible. Working on bytes means the starting vocabulary is just 256 symbols. Any string in any language can then be encoded, so there is never an unknown token. The regex (regular expression, a pattern that describes kinds of text) first splits the text into runs of letters, digits, punctuation and spaces. Merges are never allowed to cross those boundaries. Without the regex, byte pair encoding (BPE) would learn wasteful tokens such as "dog." and "dog!" separately. GPT-4 (generative pre trained transformer, version 4) also limits runs of digits to three, so numbers split more regularly.
deep: A character level base would need over 100K Unicode code points and still miss rare ones; bytes cover everything, at the cost that non ASCII characters start as 2 to 4 bytes ("é" is 2 bytes) and need merges to become one token. GPT-2's split pattern separates contractions, letter runs, digit runs, punctuation and whitespace; GPT-4's (`cl100k_base`, reproduced in minbpe `regex.py`) adds case insensitive contractions, caps number chunks with `\p{N}{1,3}` and handles newlines. BPE runs within each chunk, so merges never fuse a word with following punctuation.
say: Bytes give a base vocabulary of just 256 symbols that covers every possible string, so you never need an unknown token; the cost is that non Latin characters start out as two to four bytes each. The regex pre split chops text into categories, letters, digits, punctuation and whitespace, before BPE runs, and merges only happen inside a chunk. That stops the tokeniser from wasting vocabulary on variants like dog with a period or dog with an exclamation mark. GPT-4's pattern also caps digit runs at three, so long numbers split more consistently.
must_mention: non ASCII starts as several bytes
GPT-4 caps digit runs at three

followups.q: How many bytes is a typical emoji in UTF-8?
followups.a: Four, so before merges it costs four byte tokens.

q: How are special tokens handled, and why do tokenisers refuse to parse them from user text by default?
plain: A special token is a reserved token with a fixed job, and tokenisers block users from typing one by default. Examples are `<|endoftext|>`, which marks a document boundary, and chat role markers, which show who is speaking. Special tokens get reserved id numbers outside the merges learned by byte pair encoding (BPE). The application inserts special tokens, and they are never learned from text. Suppose the tokeniser turned the literal string `<|endoftext|>` typed in a user's message into the real special id. Then a user could fake a document boundary or pretend to be the assistant. So tiktoken (OpenAI's tokeniser library) and minbpe (Karpathy's teaching tokeniser) raise an error by default when user text contains one. You must explicitly allow special tokens when you really mean to use them.
deep: Ids for special tokens come after the merges: minbpe's README notes that with `vocab_size=32768`, the first special token gets id 32768; GPT-4's `<|endoftext|>` is 100257. minbpe's `encode(text, allowed_special="none_raise")` asserts no special string appears; `"all"` or an explicit set splits the text on special strings first and maps them to their ids, encoding the rest normally. Chat templates rely on these ids to separate system, user and assistant turns, so accidental parsing of user supplied markers is a prompt injection vector. Fine tuning that adds new special tokens must also resize the embedding and output matrices.
say: Special tokens like end of text, or the markers that separate system, user and assistant turns, get reserved ids after the regular merges, and the application inserts them deliberately. The danger is parsing them out of untrusted text: if a user types the literal string for end of text and the tokeniser maps it to the real id, they can forge document boundaries or fake an assistant turn. That's why tiktoken and minbpe, by default, raise an error if the text contains a special token string, and you have to opt in explicitly. Adding new special tokens also means resizing the embedding matrix.
must_mention: parsing user text is an injection risk
tiktoken and minbpe raise by default

followups.q: What id does GPT-4 use for <|endoftext|>?
followups.a: 100257 in cl100k_base, as shown in the minbpe README.

q: Compare BPE, WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece.
plain: Byte pair encoding (BPE), WordPiece and Unigram differ in how they choose tokens, and SentencePiece is a tool that runs two of them. BPE and WordPiece both build the vocabulary (the list of tokens) by merging pairs of tokens, and BPE merges the most frequent pair. WordPiece merges the pair that appears together most often compared with how common its two parts are. BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) uses WordPiece. Unigram works the other way: it starts with a huge list of candidate tokens and removes the ones that matter least. Google's T5 (text to text transfer transformer) model uses Unigram. SentencePiece is a library that runs BPE or Unigram straight on raw text. SentencePiece treats the space as an ordinary symbol, which helps languages like Japanese that do not use spaces.
deep:
| | BPE | WordPiece | Unigram |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direction | Bottom up merges | Bottom up merges | Top down pruning |
| Selection | Most frequent pair | Max $\frac{f(ab)}{f(a)f(b)}$ | Drop tokens whose removal raises loss least, often 10 to 20 percent per round |
| Inference | Replay merges | Greedy longest match, `##` marks continuation | Most likely segmentation, can sample |
| Users | GPT, Llama, Mistral, Qwen | BERT, DistilBERT, Electra | T5, ALBERT, XLNet |

SentencePiece encodes spaces as `▁` and needs no pre tokeniser; Llama 2 used SentencePiece BPE with byte fallback, Llama 3 moved to a 128K tiktoken based BPE. In the Hugging Face docs example, WordPiece prefers "g"+"s" (score 0.05) over "u"+"g" (0.028) even though "ug" is more frequent, because "g" and "s" co occur more than chance predicts.
say: BPE and WordPiece both grow a vocabulary bottom up by merging pairs. BPE takes the most frequent pair. WordPiece, which BERT uses, takes the pair whose joint count is highest relative to the counts of its parts, so it's closer to pointwise mutual information. Unigram goes top down: start with a large candidate set and prune the tokens whose removal hurts corpus likelihood least, and at inference it picks the most probable segmentation, which also lets you sample segmentations. SentencePiece isn't a fourth algorithm; it's a library that runs BPE or Unigram on raw text with the space as a symbol.
must_mention: Unigram prunes from a large vocabulary
SentencePiece is a library, space as a symbol

followups.q: Which does Llama 3 use?
followups.a: A tiktoken based byte level BPE with 128K tokens, replacing Llama 2's SentencePiece model.

traps: Calling SentencePiece an algorithm distinct from BPE and Unigram.

q: What are the trade offs of a larger vocabulary?
plain: A bigger vocabulary (the list of all tokens) packs the same text into fewer tokens, but it has costs. Fewer tokens means each forward pass (one run of the model over the input) covers more text. Fewer tokens also means more text fits into the context window (the most tokens the model can read at once). For example, Llama 3 moved from a 32,000 token vocabulary to 128,000. With the bigger vocabulary, English went from about 3.2 to 3.9 characters per token. The costs are bigger input and output tables and a more expensive final softmax (the step that turns scores into probabilities). Rare tokens are seen so seldom that their vectors (the lists of numbers that represent them) stay poorly trained. Small models feel the table cost most, because the tables make up a large share of their size.
deep: Benefits: compression 3.17 to 3.94 characters per token for English (Llama 3 paper), cheaper documents, longer effective context, better non English coverage (Llama 3 added 28K non English tokens). Costs: embedding and unembedding each $V\times d$; at $V = 128{,}000$, $d = 4096$ that is 524M parameters each, about 6.5 percent of an 8B model each; output matmul and softmax cost $O(Vd)$ per position; rare tokens get few gradient updates (undertrained or glitch tokens). Pad $V$ to a multiple of 64 or 128 for kernel efficiency: build-nanogpt pads 50,257 to 50,304.
say: A larger vocabulary compresses text better, so the same document takes fewer tokens, which means less compute per document and more effective context. Llama 3 went from Llama 2's 32 thousand tokens to 128 thousand and English compression improved from about 3.2 to 3.9 characters per token. The costs sit at the edges of the model: the embedding and output matrices grow linearly with vocabulary size, the softmax gets more expensive, and rare tokens barely get trained. For a small model the embedding is a big share of parameters, so small models pick smaller vocabularies or tie the matrices.
must_mention: embedding and output matrices grow with V

followups.q: Why did Karpathy pad GPT-2's vocabulary to 50,304?
followups.a: It is a multiple of 64 and 128, which GPU kernels handle faster; the extra rows are never used.

traps: Saying a bigger vocabulary is always better.

q: Why can't an LLM reliably count the r's in "strawberry", and what other quirks come from tokenisation?
plain: The model cannot see letters, because "strawberry" reaches it as just two or three token ids (whole number labels for chunks of text). To count the r's, it must have memorised how each token is spelled. The model often has not memorised spellings that precisely, so it gets the count wrong. The same root cause makes arithmetic hard, because numbers get split into uneven chunks. Tokenisation also means text in languages other than English costs more tokens per word. Even a trailing space (a space at the very end) in a prompt changes what the model sees. The reason is that " hello" with a leading space and "hello" without one are different tokens.
deep:
Quirks traced to the tokeniser (Karpathy, "Let's build the GPT Tokenizer"):

- **Spelling and counting:** letter level questions need memorised spellings of tokens.
- **Arithmetic:** inconsistent digit chunking misaligns place values; GPT-4's pattern caps chunks at three digits.
- **Non English:** under represented scripts fragment into many tokens, costing more and filling context faster.
- **Whitespace:** leading spaces are part of tokens; trailing spaces in prompts push the model to rare boundaries. GPT-2 spent a token per indentation space in Python.
- **Glitch tokens:** frequent in the tokeniser's corpus but rare in the model's (Karpathy's example "SolidGoldMagikarp"), so their embeddings are untrained and produce bizarre output.
say: Because the model doesn't see characters. Strawberry arrives as maybe two or three token ids, and to count the r's the model has to have memorised how each of those tokens is spelled, which it often hasn't precisely. The same root cause explains other quirks: arithmetic suffers because numbers get chopped into uneven chunks, non English text costs more tokens per word, a trailing space in a prompt lands the model on a rare token boundary, and a few tokens that were common in the tokeniser's data but rare in training have essentially untrained embeddings and cause strange output.
must_mention: leading spaces are part of tokens

followups.q: How would you get the right count anyway?
followups.a: Ask it to spell the word with separators first, or let it call a tool such as code execution.

traps: Saying the model simply cannot reason.

q: How does a transformer turn token ids into vectors?
plain: The transformer looks up each token id in a learned table, and the matching row of numbers is that token's vector. The table is called the embedding matrix (a grid of numbers), and it has one row for every token in the vocabulary. For example, token number 4,000 simply becomes row 4,000 of the table. Each row is a list of numbers, such as 768 values in GPT-2 small (the smallest generative pre trained transformer 2). During training, these rows move so that tokens used in similar ways end up with similar vectors. Only the rows for tokens that appear in a batch (a group of training examples) get updated in that step.
deep: $E \in \mathbb{R}^{V\times d}$; lookup of id $i$ returns $E_i$, mathematically $\text{onehot}(i)^\top E$, which is why gradients are sparse over rows. GPT-2 small: $V = 50{,}257$, $d = 768$, so $E$ has 38.6M parameters. GPT-2 also adds a learned position embedding of shape (1024, 768) before the first block (nanoGPT `wte` plus `wpe`); RoPE models add nothing at the input. Similarity between token vectors is usually measured by cosine similarity (CME295 cheatsheet). The original transformer multiplied embeddings by $\sqrt{d_{\text{model}}}$.
say: Each token id indexes a row of a learned embedding matrix with one row per vocabulary entry, so the id just selects a vector, 768 numbers in GPT-2 small. Mathematically it's a one hot vector times the matrix, which is why only the rows of tokens present in a batch receive gradient. The rows are trained along with everything else, so tokens used in similar contexts end up close together. In GPT-2 a learned position vector is added at this point; Llama style models inject position later, inside attention.
must_mention: lookup table of V rows by d columns
same as one hot times matrix

followups.q: How big is GPT-2 small's embedding table?
followups.a: 50,257 by 768, about 38.6 million parameters.

q: How does the model turn its final hidden state into a next token prediction, and what loss does it train on?
plain: The model turns its last vector into one score for every vocabulary token, then turns those scores into probabilities. After the last block (one repeated layer of the transformer), the final vector for a position is multiplied by an output matrix (a grid of numbers). The output matrix has one column per vocabulary token, so the result is one score per token, called a logit. A softmax (a function that turns scores into positive numbers that add up to one) converts the scores into probabilities. Training uses cross entropy, a loss (a score for how surprised the model is by the true answer). Cross entropy is the negative log of the probability given to the true next token, averaged over positions. For example, if the model gives the right token probability 0.5, that position's loss is about 0.69.
deep:
Logits $z_t = h_t W_U$, $W_U \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times V}$, after a final norm. Loss:
$$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\operatorname{softmax}(z_t)_{x_{t+1}}$$
which is the CME295 cheatsheet's $-\sum_i y_i\log p_i$ with one hot $y$. Perplexity $= e^{\mathcal{L}}$, the effective number of equally likely choices; loss 3.0 means perplexity about 20. One causal forward pass over $T$ tokens gives $T$ predictions. At inference nanoGPT computes logits only for the last position. CS229 Lecture 13 builds LLMs from this next word prediction loss.
say: After the final norm, each position's hidden vector is multiplied by an output matrix with one column per vocabulary token, which gives a logit for every possible next token. A softmax turns the logits into a probability distribution. The training loss is cross entropy: minus the log probability the model assigned to the token that actually came next, averaged over every position in the batch. Exponentiating the loss gives perplexity, roughly how many tokens the model is choosing between, so a loss of three is a perplexity of about twenty.
must_mention: output matrix d by V gives logits
cross entropy is minus log prob of true token

followups.q: Why does one forward pass give many training examples?
followups.a: With a causal mask, every position predicts its own next token, so a sequence of T tokens gives T predictions.

q: What loss should an untrained GPT-2 start at, and why is that a useful check?
plain: An untrained GPT-2 (generative pre trained transformer, version 2) should start at a loss (the number that measures its error) of about 10.8. An untrained model should be equally unsure about every token, so each of GPT-2's 50,257 tokens gets a probability of about 1 in 50,257. The loss is minus the log of that probability, which is the natural log of 50,257, about 10.8. The natural log is the log that uses the constant e as its base. If your first training step shows a much larger loss, the starting outputs are too confident. Too much confidence at the start points to a problem with the initialisation (how the weights are first set) or the rest of the setup. So the starting loss is a useful sanity check before a long training run. Andrej Karpathy uses exactly this check in his GPT-2 reproduction.
deep: Uniform prediction gives $-\ln(1/V) = \ln V$. GPT-2: $\ln 50257 = 10.82$; Llama 3's 128,000 vocabulary: $\ln 128000 = 11.76$. A loss well above $\ln V$ at step 0 means logits have large variance at init (for example weight std too large), so the softmax is confidently wrong. nanoGPT initialises weights with std 0.02, which keeps initial logits small. A related check: overfitting a single batch should drive the loss towards 0 quickly; if it cannot, the model or loss is buggy.
say: At initialisation the model hasn't learned anything, so ideally it spreads probability evenly over the vocabulary. For GPT-2 that's one in 50,257 per token, and the cross entropy is the natural log of 50,257, about 10.8. So when I start a run I check that the first loss is close to that. If it's much higher, the initial logits are too large and the model is confidently wrong, which usually means the initialisation scale is off. Another quick sanity check is that the model can overfit a single batch.
must_mention: much higher means logits too large

followups.q: What would the starting loss be for Llama 3's vocabulary?

q: What is weight tying, why does it help, and why do many large models not use it?
plain: Weight tying means the model uses one table of vectors for both reading tokens in and scoring tokens out. The input embedding table (one vector per token) is reused as the output matrix (the grid that scores each token). So the same vector that represents "cat" on the way in also scores "cat" as the next token. Tying saves parameters (the numbers the model learns). In GPT-2 small (generative pre trained transformer 2), the shared table is 38.6 million of 124 million numbers, about a third. Tying also helps rare tokens, because the output side updates every row of the table at every step. Large models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 usually keep two separate tables. At their size, tying would save only a few percent of the parameters.
deep: Tying sets $W_U = E^\top$ (Press and Wolf 2016; the original transformer also shared these weights). Through the softmax, every vocabulary row of $W_U$ gets gradient at every position, while input rows only learn when their token appears, so tying improves rare token embeddings and regularises. nanoGPT: `self.transformer.wte.weight = self.lm_head.weight`. Mistral 7B, Mixtral 8x7B, Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B set `tie_word_embeddings: false`; for Mistral, untying costs $32000\times4096 = 131$M parameters, 1.8 percent of 7.24B.
say: Weight tying means the embedding matrix that maps tokens to vectors is reused, transposed, as the output matrix that scores the next token. The intuition is that a token's input meaning and output meaning should be similar. It helps because the output side gets gradient for every vocabulary row at every step, while an input row only learns when its token appears, so rare tokens get better vectors. In GPT-2 small it saves about a third of the parameters. Big models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 usually untie, because the embedding is a small share and separate matrices give more freedom.
must_mention: same matrix for input and output
saves about 31 percent of GPT-2 small

followups.q: How do you check whether a model ties its embeddings?
followups.a: Look at tie_word_embeddings in its Hugging Face config, or check whether the two tensors share storage.

traps: Saying weight tying is required for the model to work.

q: What do the query, key and value vectors in attention represent?
plain: Each token makes three vectors (lists of numbers): a query, a key and a value. A token makes the query, key and value by multiplying its own embedding (its list of numbers) with three learned matrices (grids of numbers). The query says what the token is looking for. The key says what the token offers to others. The value is the information the token hands over if it is chosen. A token scores every other token by comparing its query with their keys, then takes a weighted blend of their values. In "the animal didn't cross the street because it was tired", the query for "it" should match the key for "animal" strongly.
deep: For token vectors $x$: $q = xW_Q$, $k = xW_K$, $v = xW_V$. The score $q_i\cdot k_j$ measures how relevant token $j$ is to token $i$; softmax over $j$ turns scores into weights; the output is $\sum_j a_{ij}v_j$. Separating keys from values lets the model decide relevance in one subspace and pass content in another. Karpathy frames it as communication: tokens are nodes that broadcast keys and values and pull information with queries. The CME295 cheatsheet frames it as a query choosing which key to pay attention to with respect to its value.
say: Every token makes three vectors by multiplying its embedding by three learned matrices. The query is what this token is looking for, the key is what it advertises about itself, and the value is the content it passes along if someone attends to it. To update a token, you compare its query against every key with a dot product, turn those scores into weights with a softmax, and take the weighted average of the values. It's like a soft dictionary lookup where the match is fuzzy and you get a blend instead of one entry.
must_mention: query is what I am looking for

followups.q: Why not use the same vector for key and value?
followups.a: Separating them lets the model match on one kind of feature and transmit a different kind of content.

q: Write the scaled dot product attention formula and walk through it with shapes.
plain: Scaled dot product attention turns a stack of token vectors into one new vector per token, in a few matrix steps. First, stack the token vectors into a matrix X (a grid of numbers) with T rows (one per token) and d columns (the vector size). Multiply X by three learned matrices to get the queries Q, the keys K and the values V. Multiply Q by K transposed (K with its rows and columns swapped) to get a T by T table of match scores. Divide those scores by the square root of the key size, then mask out (hide) the positions that must not be seen. Apply a softmax (which turns scores into weights that add up to one) to each row. Multiply the weights by V to get one output vector per token. With 5 tokens, the score table is 5 by 5.
deep:
$$Q = XW_Q,\ K = XW_K,\ V = XW_V,\qquad \operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)V$$
$X\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}$, $W_Q, W_K\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_k}$, $W_V\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_v}$; scores $\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times T}$; softmax over the key axis (each row sums to 1); output $\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d_v}$. $M$ holds 0 or $-\infty$ (Vaswani et al. 2017). With batches and heads, shapes are `(B, n_head, T, head_size)` as in nanoGPT. Cost: $O(T^2 d_k)$ for scores and mixing.
say: Starting from the token matrix, T tokens by d dimensions, I multiply by three learned matrices to get queries, keys and values. Then I take queries times keys transposed, which gives a T by T matrix of match scores, divide by the square root of the key dimension, add the mask so a token can't see the future, and softmax each row so its weights sum to one. The output is those weights times the values, so each token becomes a weighted mix of the values it attended to. With heads and batches the tensors are batch by heads by T by head size.

QK transpose gives T by T scores
divide by square root of d_k

followups.q: Which axis does the softmax run over?
followups.a: The key axis, so each query's weights sum to one.

traps: Applying the softmax over the query axis.

q: How can you build self attention up from simple averaging, as in Karpathy's GPT lecture?
plain: You can build self attention by starting from simple averaging and then letting the weights depend on the content. The simplest way for a token to use its past is to average the vectors of all earlier tokens. The average of earlier tokens equals a matrix multiply with a lower triangular matrix (numbers only on and below the diagonal). Each row of the lower triangular matrix adds up to one. Filling the future positions with minus infinity and applying a softmax (scores into weights) to zeros gives the same matrix. Self attention replaces the zeros with learned query and key scores. So each token chooses how much to take from each earlier token.
deep: Version 1: for loops computing $\bar{x}_t = \frac{1}{t}\sum_{s\le t}x_s$. Version 2: $W = \operatorname{tril}(\mathbf{1})$ row normalised, output $WX$. Version 3: $W = \operatorname{softmax}(\text{masked\_fill}(0, -\infty))$, identical to version 2. Version 4: replace the zeros with data dependent affinities $QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$, then output $WV$. The trick is that a matrix multiply with a row stochastic lower triangular matrix is a weighted aggregation of the past, and attention makes the weights depend on content. Karpathy also notes attention has no notion of space (it operates over sets) and no communication across the batch dimension.
say: Karpathy builds it in four steps. First, each token just averages all previous tokens' vectors, written with for loops. Second, he shows that's the same as multiplying by a lower triangular matrix whose rows sum to one. Third, you get that same matrix by putting minus infinity above the diagonal, zeros elsewhere, and taking a softmax, which gives uniform weights over the past. The final step is the key idea: replace those zeros with learned query key dot products, so the weights depend on the content and each token decides how much to take from each earlier token.
must_mention: softmax of masked zeros gives uniform weights
replace zeros with query key scores

followups.q: What does attention know about token order on its own?
followups.a: Nothing; it operates over sets, which is why positions must be added.

q: Why is the dot product divided by the square root of d_k?
plain: Dividing by the square root of the key size keeps the scores from growing too large as the vectors get longer. A dot product (multiply matching entries of two vectors and add them up) adds one small product per dimension. So the more dimensions there are, the more widely the total swings. With 128 dimensions, the raw scores spread about 11 times wider than a single product. Big scores make the softmax (the step that turns scores into weights) put almost all the weight on one token. Then nudging the scores barely changes anything, so learning stalls. Dividing by the square root of the dimension shrinks the spread back to about 1.
deep: If $q_i, k_i$ are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, then $q\cdot k = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k}q_ik_i$ has mean 0 and variance $d_k$ (Vaswani et al. 2017, footnote 1), because each term has variance $\mathbb{E}[q_i^2]\mathbb{E}[k_i^2] = 1$. Since $\operatorname{Var}(s/c) = \operatorname{Var}(s)/c^2$, dividing by $\sqrt{d_k}$ gives variance 1. The softmax Jacobian $\operatorname{diag}(p) - pp^\top$ goes to zero as $p$ approaches one hot, so unscaled scores give vanishing gradients. Simulated: variances 16, 63.8, 254.6 for $d_k = 16, 64, 256$, all about 1.0 after scaling; with $d_k = 256$ the largest of 8 softmax weights was 1.0 unscaled and 0.417 scaled.
say: Because the variance of a dot product grows with dimension. If query and key entries are roughly independent with unit variance, their dot product is a sum of d_k terms each with variance one, so its variance is d_k and its standard deviation is the square root of d_k. With d_k of 128 the scores swing by about 11, the softmax becomes nearly one hot, and its gradient is close to zero, so training stalls. Dividing by the square root of d_k brings the variance back to one. It's the square root rather than d_k because dividing by a constant divides variance by its square.
must_mention: variance of q dot k equals d_k
square root because variance scales with the square

followups.q: Is this the only fix?
followups.a: Some models also normalise queries and keys (QK norm) to control logit growth, but the square root scale is near universal.

traps: Saying it is only to prevent numerical overflow.
Saying divide by d_k.

q: Implement a numerically stable softmax. What can go wrong in attention?
plain: A numerically stable softmax subtracts the largest score in each row before doing anything else. A softmax is the function that turns scores into probabilities, using exponentials (powers of the constant e). Subtracting the same constant from every input leaves the softmax answer unchanged. After the shift, the biggest exponential is exactly 1, so nothing overflows (grows too large for the computer to store). Without the shift, scores like 1000 overflow to infinity and the output becomes NaN (not a number). For example, the scores 1000, 1001 and 1002 give the weights about 0.09, 0.245 and 0.665 once shifted. In attention you must also mask (hide the positions that must not be seen) before the softmax, and watch for rows where every position is masked.
deep:
```python
import numpy as np
def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
    e = np.exp(x)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
print(softmax(np.array([1000.0, 1001.0, 1002.0])).round(3))   # [0.09  0.245 0.665]
```
$\operatorname{softmax}(x) = \operatorname{softmax}(x - c)$ for any constant $c$. In bf16, compute the softmax in fp32. A fully masked row has max $-\infty$, giving $-\infty - (-\infty) = $ NaN, so kernels special case it. FlashAttention extends the max trick across blocks with a running maximum. A techinterview.org inference prep guide notes candidates often forget the max subtraction under pressure.
say: The standard trick is to subtract the row maximum before exponentiating. Softmax is unchanged when you add a constant to every input, and after the shift the largest exponent is e to the zero, so nothing overflows. Without it, scores in the hundreds overflow and you get NaNs. In attention there are two more traps: the mask has to go on before the softmax so each row still sums to one, and a row where every key is masked has a maximum of minus infinity, which produces NaN, so it needs special handling. FlashAttention reuses the same max trick with a running maximum.
must_mention: softmax invariant to a constant shift

followups.q: Why compute softmax in fp32 when the model runs in bf16?
followups.a: bf16 has only 7 mantissa bits, so sums of many exponentials lose precision.

q: How does the causal mask in decoder self attention work, and why is it needed?
plain: The causal mask stops each token from looking at the tokens that come after it. The mask is needed because a model learning to predict the next word could otherwise simply copy the answer. The mask sets every score for a later position to minus infinity before the softmax. The softmax (the step that turns scores into weights) then gives those later positions a weight of exactly zero. For example, in a 5 token sentence, token 3 can attend to (look at) tokens 1, 2 and 3 only. The mask lets one pass over a sentence train all of its next word predictions at once.
deep: $M_{ij} = 0$ for $j\le i$, $-\infty$ for $j > i$, added to $QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$; after softmax the upper triangle is exactly 0 and each row still sums to 1. Consequences: (1) one forward pass yields $T$ training targets; (2) the outputs at positions $< t$ do not depend on tokens $\ge t$ (in a numpy check, changing the last token left all earlier outputs unchanged), which is what makes the KV cache valid. nanoGPT uses `torch.tril` for the manual path and `is_causal=True` with `scaled_dot_product_attention`. Masking after the softmax is wrong, because rows no longer sum to 1.
say: In a decoder I add a mask to the score matrix before the softmax: zero on and below the diagonal and minus infinity above it. After the softmax those future positions get exactly zero weight, so token i only uses tokens one through i and can't cheat by looking at the word it's supposed to predict. That's what lets a single forward pass train every next token prediction in the sequence in parallel. It's also why caching works at inference, since earlier tokens never depend on later ones. The detail people get wrong is masking after the softmax instead of before.

followups.q: What would go wrong without the mask in training?
followups.a: Each position could attend to its own target token, so the model learns to copy and fails at generation.

traps: Masking after the softmax.

q: What is a padding mask, and what practical issues come with padding?
plain: A padding mask hides the filler tokens that are added so sequences of different lengths can share a batch. A batch is a group of examples processed together, so shorter sequences are filled out with padding tokens. The padding mask sets the scores for those padding positions (the keys) to minus infinity before the softmax (the step that turns scores into weights). With the mask, real tokens never attend to (look at) the padding. The padding positions still produce outputs, but the loss (the number that measures the model's error) ignores them. For example, a batch holding a 3 token and a 5 token sequence gives the short one 2 pad tokens, which are masked.
deep: Key padding mask: scores $(i, j)$ set to $-\infty$ where key $j$ is padding. Pad query rows produce garbage that is excluded via `ignore_index` in cross entropy (nanoGPT uses -1). Pitfalls: a fully masked row gives NaN; for batched generation pad on the left so every sequence's last real token is at the same index; with RoPE, position ids must skip padding. Pretraining avoids padding by packing documents end to end with an end of text separator; Llama 3 additionally masks attention across document boundaries, which it reports mattered little for standard pretraining and a lot for long context continued pretraining.
say: Padding is filler added so sequences in a batch have equal length. The padding mask puts minus infinity on the scores for padding keys, so real tokens never attend to them. The pad positions still produce outputs, but they're excluded from the loss with an ignore index. A few practical issues: a row that's entirely masked produces NaN, for batched generation you pad on the left so all sequences end at the same position, and position ids need to account for padding. In pretraining people avoid padding altogether by packing documents together, and Llama 3 also masks attention across documents within a packed sequence.
must_mention: mask pad keys with minus infinity
pad outputs ignored in the loss

followups.q: Why does Llama 3 mask across packed documents?
followups.a: So a token cannot attend to an unrelated document in the same sequence; the paper found it important for long context training.

q: What is the computational complexity of self attention, and when does it dominate the cost of a layer?
plain: Self attention's cost grows with the square of the sequence length, but it only dominates a layer for long sequences. Every token compares itself with every other token, so the work and the score table grow with the square of the length. The projections (the matrices that make queries, keys and values) grow only in proportion to the length. The feed forward network (the small network applied to each token) also grows in proportion to the length. Both the projections and the feed forward network grow with the square of the model width (the size of each token's vector). For GPT-2 small (generative pre trained transformer 2, its smallest size), attention only becomes the bigger cost past about 4,600 tokens. So at ordinary lengths the feed forward network still costs more.
deep: Per layer: $QK^\top$ and $AV$ cost about $4T^2d$ FLOPs and the score matrix needs $O(T^2)$ memory per head; the four projections and a $4d$ FFN cost about $24Td^2$. Attention dominates when $T > 6d$: 4,608 tokens at $d = 768$, about 24,600 at $d = 4096$. Versus recurrence: $O(1)$ sequential operations and $O(1)$ maximum path length between positions, against $O(T)$ (Vaswani et al. 2017, Table 1). At decode with a KV cache each new token costs $O(Td)$ for attention over the cache.
say: Self attention is quadratic in sequence length: the score matrix is T by T per head, so time is order T squared times d, and memory for the scores is order T squared unless you use FlashAttention. The projections and feed forward network are order T times d squared. Working it through with the usual four times wide FFN, attention only dominates when T exceeds about six times d, which is around 4,600 tokens for GPT-2 small and 25 thousand for a 4,096 wide model. The upside over RNNs is that any two tokens are one step apart and every position is computed in parallel.
must_mention: projections and FFN are T d squared

followups.q: What does FlashAttention change about this?
followups.a: Memory becomes linear in T because the score matrix is never stored; FLOPs stay quadratic.

traps: Saying attention is always the bottleneck.

q: Implement causal self attention with an optional padding mask in numpy, and test that it is causal.
plain: Compute the scores, hide the forbidden positions, apply a stable softmax, and multiply by the values. Hiding means setting the scores for future positions and for padding (filler) keys to minus infinity. A stable softmax (the function that turns scores into weights) subtracts the largest score first, so nothing overflows (grows too big to store). To test causality, change the last token's vector and run attention again. All earlier outputs must stay exactly the same, and if any moved, information leaked from the future. For example, use a random input of 5 tokens with 8 numbers each, and add 10 to the last token's vector. In that test the first 4 outputs stay equal, so `np.allclose` returns True. Implementing this is a common warm up in machine learning coding rounds.
deep:
```python
import numpy as np
def softmax(x, axis=-1):
    x = x - x.max(axis=axis, keepdims=True); e = np.exp(x)
    return e / e.sum(axis=axis, keepdims=True)
def attention(Q, K, V, causal=True, key_padding=None):
    T, d_k = Q.shape[-2], Q.shape[-1]
    S = Q @ K.swapaxes(-1, -2) / np.sqrt(d_k)
    if causal:
        S = np.where(np.tril(np.ones((T, T), bool)), S, -np.inf)
    if key_padding is not None:
        S = np.where(key_padding[None, :], -np.inf, S)
    return softmax(S) @ V
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.standard_normal((5, 8))
Wq, Wk, Wv = (rng.standard_normal((8, 8)) / np.sqrt(8) for _ in range(3))
out = attention(X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv)
X2 = X.copy(); X2[-1] += 10
out2 = attention(X2 @ Wq, X2 @ Wk, X2 @ Wv)
print(np.allclose(out[:-1], out2[:-1]))   # True
```
say: I'd compute the scores as Q times K transposed over the square root of d_k, then use a lower triangular boolean matrix to replace future positions with minus infinity, and do the same for any padding keys. Then a softmax with the max subtracted, and multiply by V. To test it, I perturb the last token's input and assert that the outputs for every earlier position are unchanged; if any of them move, the mask is leaking the future. I'd also check shapes, that each row of weights sums to one, and that a fully masked row is handled.
must_mention: scores over square root of d_k
perturb last token to test causality

followups.q: How would you add multiple heads?
followups.a: Reshape to (heads, T, head_size), run the same function batched over heads, then concatenate and apply W_O.

topic: Multi head attention, MQA and GQA
q: Why use multiple attention heads instead of one?
plain: Several attention heads let a token pay attention to different kinds of relationships at the same time. One head gives each token a single set of weights, so it can focus sharply on only one kind of relationship. Multi head attention runs several smaller heads side by side, each working on its own slice of the vector. Multi head attention then glues (joins end to end) the outputs of all the heads together. For example, one head might track the previous word while another tracks the subject of the sentence. In GPT-2 small (generative pre trained transformer 2), 768 dimensions (numbers per token) are split into 12 heads of 64. So the total cost is the same as one wide head.
deep: $\operatorname{head}_i = \operatorname{Attention}(XW_Q^{(i)}, XW_K^{(i)}, XW_V^{(i)})$, $\operatorname{MHA}(X) = [\operatorname{head}_1;\dots;\operatorname{head}_h]W_O$, $d_{\text{head}} = d/h$. The original base transformer: $d = 512$, $h = 8$, $d_k = 64$ (Vaswani et al. 2017). Each softmax is one distribution per query, so $h$ heads give $h$ independent attention patterns at no extra parameter or FLOP cost. Heads specialise empirically (positional, induction, syntactic heads) and many can be pruned at inference with little loss.
say: One head gives each token a single softmax distribution over the other tokens, so it can really only focus sharply in one way at a time. With multiple heads, each working in a smaller subspace, one head can look at the previous token, another at a matching bracket, another at the subject of the sentence, all in parallel. It costs nothing extra: you split the same width into, say, 12 heads of 64 dimensions, so parameters and FLOPs match a single wide head. The output projection then mixes the heads back together.

followups.q: How are the head outputs combined?
followups.a: Concatenated back to width d and multiplied by the output matrix W_O.

traps: Saying more heads means more parameters.

topic: Multi head attention, MQA and GQA
q: How many parameters does multi head attention have, and how is it implemented efficiently?
plain: Standard multi head attention has four weight matrices of size d by d, where d is the width of each token's vector. The four matrices handle the queries, the keys, the values and the output. The total is 4 times d squared parameters (the numbers the model learns), however many heads you use. The count stays the same because the heads just split the same width between them. For GPT-2 small (generative pre trained transformer 2) with its biases (extra added numbers), one layer has 2,362,368 parameters. In code, all the heads are computed at once by reshaping the data. The heads are treated like an extra batch dimension (an extra axis of the data).
deep: Without biases $4d^2$; GPT-2 small: $768\cdot2304 + 2304 + 768\cdot768 + 768 = 2{,}362{,}368$. nanoGPT computes one fused $d\times3d$ projection (`c_attn`), splits into q, k, v, reshapes each to `(B, T, n_head, head_size)` and transposes to `(B, n_head, T, head_size)`, so attention runs batched over heads; afterwards it transposes back and views as `(B, T, C)` before `c_proj`. Changing $h$ changes slicing and the size of the $T\times T$ score tensor count ($h$ of them), not the weight count.
say: Standard MHA has four d by d matrices, for queries, keys, values and the output, so four d squared parameters regardless of head count. The heads are just slices of that width. For GPT-2 small, with biases, that's about 2.36 million per layer. Efficient implementations do one fused matrix multiply that produces queries, keys and values together, reshape to batch by heads by sequence by head size, and run attention batched over the heads, then reshape back and apply the output projection. Karpathy's exercise in the GPT lecture is exactly to rewrite the per head loop this way.

followups.q: What does changing the head count change?
followups.a: The head size and number of attention patterns, not the parameter count.

q: CNNs and RNNs don't use positional embeddings. Why do transformers need them?
plain: Self attention cannot tell word order by itself, so a transformer has to be told each token's position explicitly. A recurrent network (one that reads tokens one after another) has order built into how it works. A convolution (a small filter that slides over the input) looks at fixed neighbouring positions, so it also knows order. Self attention compares all tokens with the same weights and treats them like an unordered set. If you shuffle the input words, the outputs just shuffle along with them. So "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same to it.
deep: Without position information, self attention is permutation equivariant: $\operatorname{Attn}(PX) = P\operatorname{Attn}(X)$ for a permutation matrix $P$, so order carries no signal. A causal mask does break the symmetry (each position sees a different prefix), but models still use explicit positions. Options: add absolute vectors to embeddings (sinusoidal, learned), add relative biases to scores (T5, ALiBi), or rotate queries and keys (RoPE). Recurrence encodes order through sequential state; convolution through kernels with fixed relative offsets.
say: Because attention by itself treats the input as a set. Every token scores every other token with the same weights, so if you shuffle the words the outputs just shuffle with them, and the model can't tell dog bites man from man bites dog. An RNN gets order from processing one step at a time, and a CNN gets it from kernels that look at fixed relative offsets. So transformers inject position explicitly: by adding a position vector to each embedding, by adding a distance based bias to the attention scores, or by rotating queries and keys, which is RoPE.

followups.q: Is attention permutation invariant or equivariant?
followups.a: Equivariant: permuting inputs permutes outputs the same way.

traps: Saying attention is permutation invariant.

q: What are learned absolute position embeddings, and what is their main limitation?
plain: A learned absolute position embedding is a table with one trainable vector for each position. The position vector is added to each token's embedding (its list of numbers) before the first block (the first repeated layer of the transformer). For example, GPT-2 (generative pre trained transformer, version 2) has 1,024 rows, so position 7 always gets row 7. BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) has 512 rows. A learned position table is simple and works well within the length it was trained on. The main weakness is that the table has no row for position 1,025, so the model cannot handle longer inputs. Positions near the end of the table are also trained less often.
deep: GPT-2 / nanoGPT: `wpe = nn.Embedding(block_size, n_embd)`, `x = wte(idx) + wpe(arange(T))`, 1024 × 768 = 786,432 parameters. BERT: 512 positions. Vaswani et al. (2017) found learned and sinusoidal embeddings gave nearly identical results. Limitations: hard maximum length (nanoGPT asserts `t <= block_size` and crops context at generation), no built in notion of relative distance, rarely seen late positions. nanoGPT's `crop_block_size` can shrink the table but never extend it.
say: Learned absolute positions are just a second embedding table, one trainable vector per position, that gets added to the token embedding at the input. GPT-2 has 1,024 of them and BERT 512. It's simple and in the original transformer paper it performed about as well as sinusoids. The big limitation is the hard cap: there's no vector for position 1,025, so you can't run longer sequences without retraining, and the model has no built in sense that positions 10 and 11 are close. That's a big reason newer models moved to relative or rotary schemes.

followups.q: What does nanoGPT do when generation exceeds the block size?
followups.a: It crops the context to the last block_size tokens.

q: Write the sinusoidal positional encoding and explain why it was chosen.
plain: Sinusoidal positional encoding is what the original transformer adds to each token to show its position. The encoding is a fixed pattern of sine and cosine waves (smooth up and down curves). Each pair of dimensions (numbers in the vector) oscillates (swings up and down) at a different speed, like the hands of many clocks. Fast waves tell neighbouring positions apart, and slow waves tell distant positions apart. A key property is that moving any position forward by a fixed amount, say 5, is the same rotation for every starting position. A rotation here means turning each pair of wave values by a fixed angle. For example, shifting by 5 takes position 7 to 12 and position 40 to 45 with the same rotation. The authors hoped the rotation property would make relative positions (the gaps between tokens) easy to learn and allow longer inputs than seen in training.
deep:
$$PE_{(pos,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right),\quad PE_{(pos,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)$$
Wavelengths form a geometric series from $2\pi$ to $10000\cdot2\pi$. For fixed $k$, $PE_{pos+k} = M_k PE_{pos}$ with $M_k$ block diagonal $2\times2$ rotations; verified numerically for $k = 5$ from positions 7 and 40. Vaswani et al. (2017) chose it because it "may allow the model to extrapolate" to longer sequences, and found learned embeddings nearly identical. In practice extrapolation was poor, which motivated relative methods.
say: Each pair of dimensions gets a sine and a cosine of the position at a different frequency, with frequencies falling geometrically from one cycle every six or so tokens to one every sixty thousand. So it's like a set of clocks running at different speeds, and each position has a unique reading. The nice property is that shifting by a fixed offset is the same linear map, a rotation in each pair, from any starting point, which the authors thought would make relative attention easy and might allow extrapolation. In practice it didn't extrapolate well, which led to ALiBi and RoPE.
must_mention: sine and cosine at geometric frequencies
shift by k is a fixed rotation

followups.q: Did sinusoidal encodings actually extrapolate well?
followups.a: Not reliably; ALiBi's paper showed sinusoidal models degrade beyond the trained length.

q: What are the T5 relative bias and ALiBi?
plain: The T5 (text to text transfer transformer) relative bias and ALiBi (attention with linear biases) both put position into the attention scores. Both methods work on the scores instead of adding position to the embeddings (the token vectors). T5 learns one small number for each range of distances between two tokens. T5 adds the learned number to the attention score of those two tokens. ALiBi has no learned parameters (numbers the model adjusts during training). Instead ALiBi subtracts a penalty that grows in proportion to the distance, with a different slope in each head. So nearby tokens score higher than far away ones. A model trained with ALiBi on 1,024 token inputs handled 2,048 tokens as well as a sinusoidal model (fixed sine wave positions) trained on 2,048.
deep: T5: bias $b_{\text{bucket}(i-j)}$ shared across layers, with log spaced buckets for long distances. ALiBi (Press, Smith and Lewis 2021): score $q_i\cdot k_j - m_h(i - j)$, slopes $m_h$ a geometric sequence across heads, nothing added to embeddings. Results: a 1.3B model trained at length 1,024 and tested at 2,048 matched the perplexity of a sinusoidal model trained at 2,048, while training 11 percent faster and using 11 percent less memory. Trade off: a built in recency bias that can hurt tasks needing distant information. CME295 Lecture 2 covers both.
say: Both move position from the input into the attention scores. T5 learns a scalar bias for each bucket of relative distance, with buckets growing logarithmically for far distances, and adds it to the score. ALiBi is even simpler: no learned parameters, it just subtracts the distance times a fixed slope, with each head getting a different slope so some heads look locally and others further. The headline result was train short, test long: a model trained on 1,024 tokens matched a sinusoidal model trained on 2,048 when tested at 2,048. The cost is a strong bias toward recent tokens.

followups.q: Why can ALiBi extrapolate?
followups.a: The penalty is defined for any distance, so longer inputs only produce larger, familiar looking penalties.

q: What is RoPE, in plain terms?
plain: RoPE (rotary position embedding) tells the model where each token is by rotating its query and key vectors. The angle of rotation grows with the token's position. Llama, Mistral and Qwen all use it. The model compares a query and a key with a dot product (multiply matching entries and add them up). After rotation, only the difference between their two angles matters, and that depends only on how far apart the tokens are. So a query at position 3 and a key at position 10 score the same as that pair at positions 103 and 110. Values are not rotated, and nothing is added to the embeddings (the token vectors).
deep: RoPE (Su et al. 2021) applies a position dependent rotation $R_{\Theta,m}$ to $q_m$ and $k_m$ inside every attention layer. Because $R_m^\top R_n = R_{n-m}$, the score $q_m^\top k_n$ depends on positions only through $n - m$, giving relative position from an absolute operation. A numerical check confirmed $\langle R_3q, R_{10}k\rangle = \langle R_{103}q, R_{110}k\rangle$ and $\ne\langle R_3q, R_{11}k\rangle$. CME295 cheatsheet: RoPE rotates query and key vectors to incorporate relative position information. Llama 3 sets the base to 500,000 for longer contexts.
say: RoPE encodes position by rotating the query and key vectors, in many two dimensional planes, by an angle proportional to the token's position. The trick is that when you take the dot product of a rotated query and a rotated key, the two rotations combine into one rotation by the difference in positions. So the attention score depends on how far apart the tokens are, not on where they sit, which is relative position for free. It's applied to queries and keys in every layer, values are untouched, and nothing is added to the residual stream. Llama, Mistral and Qwen all use it.
must_mention: rotate queries and keys by position
dot product depends on the offset

followups.q: Where exactly is RoPE applied?
followups.a: To queries and keys inside each attention layer, after the projections.

traps: Saying RoPE is added to the input embeddings.

source.title: techinterview.org, What LLM interviewers actually ask about transformers

q: Derive why RoPE makes attention scores depend only on relative position.
plain: In RoPE (rotary position embedding), the dot product of a rotated query and key depends only on the difference of their angles. Think of each pair of numbers in a query as a point on a flat plane. Rotate that point by an angle equal to its position times a fixed speed. Now rotate the query by angle a and the key by angle b. Then take their dot product (multiply matching entries and add them up). The result is the same as leaving the query alone and rotating the key by b minus a. So the score depends only on the gap between positions. Each pair of numbers uses a different speed, so some pairs track nearby distances and others track far ones.
deep:
2D case as complex numbers: $f_q(x_m, m) = (W_qx_m)e^{im\theta}$, $f_k(x_n, n) = (W_kx_n)e^{in\theta}$; the real part of $f_q\overline{f_k}$ is the dot product, with phase $e^{i(m-n)\theta}$. In $d$ dimensions: $R_{\Theta,m} = \operatorname{diag}(R(m\theta_1),\dots,R(m\theta_{d/2}))$ with $R(\phi) = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\phi & -\sin\phi\\ \sin\phi & \cos\phi\end{pmatrix}$ and $\theta_i = 10000^{-2(i-1)/d}$. Orthogonality gives $R_m^\top R_n = R_{n-m}$, so
$$(R_mW_qx_m)^\top(R_nW_kx_n) = x_m^\top W_q^\top R_{n-m}W_kx_n$$
(Su et al. 2021). The paper also shows a long term decay of the score bound with distance.
say: Take one pair of dimensions and treat it as a complex number. RoPE multiplies the query at position m by e to the i m theta and the key at position n by e to the i n theta. The dot product is the real part of the query times the conjugate of the key, and the phases combine into e to the i times m minus n times theta, so only the offset survives. In full dimension you do this independently for each of the d over two pairs with frequencies theta i equal to ten thousand to the minus two i over d. In matrix form, rotations are orthogonal, so R m transpose times R n equals R of n minus m.
must_mention: phases combine to m minus n
theta_i = 10000 to the minus 2i over d
R_m transpose R_n = R_(n minus m)

followups.q: Why does the norm of the query not change?
followups.a: Rotations are orthogonal, so RoPE preserves vector length and the score scale.

q: How is RoPE implemented in practice, and what properties matter?
plain: In practice, RoPE (rotary position embedding) is a few cheap operations on numbers, and nobody builds the rotation matrix. For each pair of numbers in a query or key, you compute the cosine and sine (basic wave functions) of position times that pair's frequency. You then combine the results, which takes only a few element wise operations (done on each number separately). The base is a constant that sets each pair's frequency (how fast it turns), and the usual value is 10,000. A wavelength is the number of tokens a pair needs for one full turn. With 128 dimensions per head, the wavelengths run from about 6 tokens to about 54,000 tokens. Raising the base, as Llama 3 does with 500,000, slows the slowest pairs so long distances stay distinguishable.
deep:
```python
import numpy as np
def rope(x, pos, base=10000.0):
    d = x.shape[-1]
    theta = base ** (-np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)
    cos, sin = np.cos(pos * theta), np.sin(pos * theta)
    x1, x2 = x[..., 0::2], x[..., 1::2]
    out = np.empty_like(x)
    out[..., 0::2] = x1 * cos - x2 * sin
    out[..., 1::2] = x1 * sin + x2 * cos
    return out
```
Equivalent to the paper's $x\odot\cos + \operatorname{rotate}(x)\odot\sin$ with rotate mapping $(x_1, x_2)\mapsto(-x_2, x_1)$; Hugging Face uses a "rotate half" layout that pairs dimension $i$ with $i + d/2$ instead of adjacent pairs, which is equivalent up to a fixed permutation of $W_Q, W_K$. Properties: norm preserving; applied to q and k only; a key's rotation depends only on its own position, so cached keys stay valid; wavelengths for $d_{\text{head}} = 128$: 6.28 to about 54,410 tokens at base 10,000, about 2.56M at base 500,000.
say: In code you never form the matrix. You precompute, for each pair index, a frequency of base to the minus two i over d, then for position p take cosine and sine of p times those frequencies, and for each pair compute x1 cos minus x2 sin and x1 sin plus x2 cos. Hugging Face pairs dimension i with i plus d over two, the rotate half layout, which is equivalent up to a permutation. Properties I'd mention: it preserves norms, it's applied to queries and keys only, cached keys stay valid because a key's rotation depends only on its own position, and the base sets the longest wavelength.
must_mention: element wise cos and sin, no matrix
frequencies base to the minus 2i over d

followups.q: What is the longest wavelength for head dimension 128 and base 10,000?
followups.a: About 54,000 tokens; with base 500,000 it is about 2.56 million.

q: How has positional encoding evolved, and why did RoPE win?
plain: Positional encoding moved from the input into the attention scores, and RoPE (rotary position embedding) ended up winning. The original transformer added fixed sine waves to the input. GPT-2 (generative pre trained transformer, version 2) learned one vector per position, capped at a fixed length. BERT (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers) did the same. T5 (text to text transfer transformer) and ALiBi (attention with linear biases) added distance based biases to the scores. RoPE rotates queries and keys so that scores depend on distance. RoPE won because it gives relative position cheaply, works with the KV (key value) cache, and stretches to longer contexts by changing its base. For example, Llama 3 raises that base (a constant that sets how fast rotations turn) to 500,000.
deep:
| Method | Where | Relative | Learned | Extrapolation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sinusoidal (Vaswani 2017) | Added to input | Indirect | No | Poor in practice |
| Learned absolute (GPT-2, BERT) | Added to input | No | Yes | None past the table |
| T5 bias | Scores | Yes | Yes | Moderate |
| ALiBi (Press 2021) | Scores | Yes | No | Good, recency biased |
| RoPE (Su 2021) | Rotates q, k | Yes | No | Needs base change or interpolation |

RoPE is the default in Llama, Mistral and Qwen; long context versions raise the base (Llama 3: 500,000) or interpolate positions.
say: It went from adding position at the input toward building it into the attention scores. The original transformer added sinusoids, and GPT-2 and BERT learned a vector per position, which caps the length. Then relative methods: T5 learned a bias per distance bucket, and ALiBi subtracts a fixed slope times distance, which extrapolates well but biases toward recent tokens. RoPE rotates queries and keys so the score depends on relative distance without any extra parameters. It won because it's cheap, works cleanly with the KV cache, and you can extend context by raising its base or interpolating positions.
must_mention: sinusoidal and learned at the input
T5 and ALiBi biases in scores

followups.q: What did ALiBi show about extrapolation?
followups.a: Trained at 1,024 tokens, it matched a sinusoidal model trained at 2,048 when tested at 2,048.

q: Walk me through one block of a modern decoder only transformer.
plain: A block in a decoder only transformer (one that predicts the next token from earlier tokens) does two steps, each wrapped the same way. First, the token vectors are normalised (rescaled to a steady size) and passed through attention. The attention result is then added back onto the original vectors. Second, the vectors are normalised again and passed through a feed forward network (a small network run on each token separately). The feed forward result is added back onto the vectors too. GPT-2 small (generative pre trained transformer, version 2) stacks 12 such blocks. Llama 3 8B (the 8 billion parameter version) stacks 32 blocks. Both models apply one final normalisation before the output layer, the part that scores every possible next token.
deep:
```text
x = x + Attention(Norm(x))
x = x + FFN(Norm(x))
```
This is nanoGPT's `Block.forward`. Llama, Mistral and Qwen use the same shape with RMSNorm, RoPE inside attention, GQA and a SwiGLU FFN, no biases in linear layers, and no dropout in pretraining (GPT-2 used dropout 0.1 per its config). After the last block: final norm, then the unembedding. Attention is the only operation that mixes information across positions; the FFN and norms act on each position separately.
say: Each block has two sublayers in sequence, both in the same pre norm residual form. First, normalise the input, run multi head attention, and add the output back to the input. Second, normalise again, run the position wise feed forward network, and add that back. Attention is where tokens exchange information; the feed forward network processes each token on its own. Modern models like Llama use RMSNorm, rotary positions inside attention, grouped query attention and a SwiGLU feed forward. Stack that 32 times, add a final norm and the output projection, and you have the model.
must_mention: attention mixes tokens, FFN per token

followups.q: Which part moves information between tokens?
followups.a: Only attention; everything else is per position.

q: What do residual connections do in a transformer, and how do they prevent vanishing gradients?
plain: A residual connection means each sublayer adds its output to its input instead of replacing it. Think of a shared notebook passed up the stack. Every layer reads the notebook and writes notes in the margin, and nothing is erased. So information from layer 2 is still there at layer 30. The training signal (the gradient, which says how to change each weight) also has a direct path back to every layer. The direct path lets a 32 or 80 layer model train without the gradient fading away, which is called the vanishing gradient problem.
deep: For $y = x + f(x)$, $\partial y/\partial x = I + \partial f/\partial x$, so the identity term carries the gradient straight through regardless of $f$. **Residual stream view:** a width $d$ stream from the embedding to the unembedding that every sublayer reads (through a norm) and writes to additively; this is the framing used in mechanistic interpretability. Karpathy's lecture describes the residual path as a gradient superhighway and adds projections back into it. Without residuals, deep stacks of attention and MLPs train poorly.
say: Residual connections mean every attention or feed forward sublayer adds its output to the running vector instead of replacing it. The derivative of x plus f of x is the identity plus the derivative of f, so there's always an identity path that carries the gradient straight back to early layers, which is how a 32 or 80 layer stack trains without vanishing gradients. I like the residual stream picture: a shared channel of width d that runs from the embedding to the output, where each layer reads from it and writes an update into it, and nothing gets overwritten.
must_mention: derivative is identity plus derivative of f

followups.q: What does the residual stream view predict about early layer information?
followups.a: It stays available to every later layer unless something writes over it additively.

source.title: LLM Interview Questions and Answers Hub (KalyanKS NLP)

q: Why does GPT-2 scale the initialisation of residual projections by one over the square root of twice the depth?
plain: The scaling keeps the sum of many random updates from growing as the model gets deeper. Every block adds two updates to the residual stream, which is the running sum that all layers write into. One update comes from attention and one from the feed forward network (a small network run on each token). After 12 blocks that is 24 random updates added together (two per block), and the sum of many random numbers grows. So GPT-2 (generative pre trained transformer, version 2) shrinks each update's starting size by one over the square root of 24. Everything else starts with a standard deviation (a typical size of the random starting values) of 0.02.
deep: nanoGPT / build-nanogpt: all Linear and Embedding weights $\sim\mathcal{N}(0, 0.02^2)$; the output projection of each residual branch (`c_proj` in attention and MLP, flagged `NANOGPT_SCALE_INIT`) uses std $0.02/\sqrt{2L}$. The stream after $L$ blocks is $x_0 + \sum_{k=1}^{2L} f_k$; if branch outputs are roughly independent with variance $\sigma^2$, the sum's variance grows like $2L\sigma^2$, so scaling each branch by $1/\sqrt{2L}$ keeps it constant. This follows the GPT-2 paper. Biases are zero initialised.
say: In GPT-2 every block adds two branches into the residual stream, attention and MLP, so a 12 layer model sums 24 branch outputs on top of the embedding. If those are roughly independent, the variance of the stream grows linearly with the number of branches. Scaling the output projection of each branch by one over the square root of two times the number of layers cancels that growth, so the stream's scale at initialisation doesn't depend on depth. Everything else in nanoGPT is initialised from a normal with standard deviation 0.02.
must_mention: variance grows with number of summed branches
scale by 1 over square root of 2L

followups.q: Which weights get the scaled init in nanoGPT?
followups.a: The c_proj output projections of attention and of the MLP.

q: Where is layer normalisation applied, and why did models move from post norm to pre norm?
plain: Modern models apply layer normalisation (rescaling each token's numbers to a steady size) before each sublayer, which is called pre norm. The original transformer normalised after adding each sublayer's output back to its input, which is called post norm. Almost every large language model (LLM) since GPT-2 (generative pre trained transformer, version 2) uses pre norm instead. Such models also add one final normalisation at the end. Pre norm keeps a clean shortcut path through the whole stack of layers. So training is more stable and less sensitive to the learning rate warmup (a slow start to the learning rate). Post norm models, by contrast, often blow up early in training without a careful warmup.
deep: Post norm: $x\leftarrow\operatorname{LN}(x + F(x))$ (Vaswani et al. 2017). Pre norm: $x\leftarrow x + F(\operatorname{LN}(x))$ plus a final LN. In post norm the residual path itself is normalised every layer, breaking the identity shortcut; Xiong et al. (2020) show the expected gradients near the output are large at initialisation, which is why post norm needs warmup. Pre norm trains stably at depth with larger learning rates. Trade off: in pre norm the stream grows and later branches contribute relatively less; tuned post norm can match or beat it when it trains.
say: In the original transformer the norm came after the residual add: layer norm of x plus the sublayer output. Almost every LLM since GPT-2 uses pre norm: normalise the input to the sublayer, add the result to the raw stream, and put one final norm before the output. The reason is stability. In post norm the shortcut path itself goes through a normalisation every layer, so there's no clean identity path, and gradients near the output are large at initialisation, which makes it very sensitive to warmup. Pre norm keeps the identity path clean and trains reliably at depth.
must_mention: post norm normalises after the add
pre norm normalises the sublayer input

followups.q: Is there any downside to pre norm?
followups.a: Later layers' updates become a smaller share of a growing stream; some argue tuned post norm ends slightly better.

traps: Saying the original transformer used pre norm.
