q: What limits how long a context an LLM can handle?
plain: Three things limit how long a context (the text the model reads at once) can be. First, attention compares every token with every other, so the work of reading the prompt grows with the square of its length. Second, the KV (key value) cache grows with every token. For Llama 3 8B, a 128,000 token context needs 16 GiB (gibibytes, slightly more than gigabytes) of cache. Third, the model only handles positions it saw during training. So a model trained on 8,000 tokens usually falls apart well beyond that unless it is adapted.
deep: Compute: prefill attention $O(T^2d)$ (FlashAttention keeps memory linear but FLOPs quadratic). Memory: KV cache $2Ln_{kv}d_{\text{head}}bT$, 128 KiB per token for Llama 3 8B. Positions: learned tables stop at their size; RoPE angles beyond the trained range are unseen, so perplexity rises past the training length. The CME295 cheatsheet puts typical context lengths at tens of thousands to millions of tokens and notes quality degrades as the window fills ("context rot"). Long prompts are also slow: prefill dominates latency for a 100K token input.
say: Three constraints. Compute: prefill attention is quadratic in length, so a 100K token prompt is expensive even with FlashAttention, which fixes memory but not FLOPs. Memory: the KV cache grows linearly, 16 gigabytes for one 128K sequence on an 8B model, which caps how many such requests a GPU can hold. And training: the model only handles positions it learned, so rotation angles or position indices beyond the training length break it unless you adapt the position encoding and continue training on long data. Then there's quality: accepting long inputs isn't the same as using them well.
must_mention: quality degrades as the window fills

followups.q: What are the pros and cons of a large context window?
followups.a: Pro: whole documents and long chats without retrieval. Con: cost, latency, cache memory and weaker use of the middle.

source.title: LLM Interview Questions and Answers Hub (KalyanKS NLP)

q: What is the lost in the middle problem?
plain: Lost in the middle means models use the start and end of a long prompt better than the middle. Models that accept very long prompts do not use all parts of them equally well. Liu and colleagues found in 2023 that answers were most accurate when the needed fact sat near the start or end of the prompt. Accuracy dropped when the fact was buried in the middle. So stuffing 50 retrieved documents into a prompt can work worse than giving the 5 most relevant ones. Simple needle in a haystack tests plant one fact and ask for it. Needle in a haystack tests overstate how well models use long contexts.
deep: Liu et al. 2023, "Lost in the Middle": U shaped accuracy as a function of the relevant document's position in multi document QA and key value retrieval. The CME295 cheatsheet calls the general degradation as the window fills "context rot". Implications: put key instructions and evidence at the start or end, rerank and trim retrieved context, evaluate with multi fact and reasoning benchmarks rather than single needle retrieval. Partial causes: training data rarely requires long range dependencies, and RoPE's long range decay biases attention toward nearby and initial tokens.
say: It's the finding from Liu and colleagues in 2023 that long context models use information at the beginning and end of the prompt much better than information in the middle, giving a U shaped accuracy curve over position. Practically, that means stuffing everything into a long window can underperform a shorter, well chosen context, so I'd rerank and trim retrieved documents and put the important material at the start or end. It also means needle in a haystack tests, which plant a single fact, overstate real long context ability, so I'd evaluate with multi fact and reasoning tasks.
must_mention: accuracy best at start and end

followups.q: What is context rot?
followups.a: The CME295 cheatsheet's name for response quality degrading as the context window fills up.

source.title: Let's Data Science, 50 LLM and AI engineer interview questions for 2026

q: How do position interpolation, NTK aware scaling and YaRN extend a RoPE model's context?
plain: Position interpolation, NTK (neural tangent kernel) aware scaling and YaRN (yet another rotary position embedding extension) all stretch positions to fit a longer context. A model using RoPE (rotary position embedding) and trained on 8,000 tokens has never seen the rotation angles that later positions produce. Position interpolation squeezes the new, longer range of positions into the trained range. For example, dividing every position by 16 takes a model from 8K to 128K tokens. Then you fine tune (train a little more) briefly. NTK aware scaling and YaRN are gentler than squeezing every position equally. NTK aware scaling and YaRN stretch the slowly rotating pairs, which encode long distances, while leaving the fast pairs, which encode word order nearby, almost unchanged. Simply raising RoPE's base frequency, as Llama 3 did, is a related way to slow the rotations.
deep: Position interpolation (Chen et al. 2023): use position $m/s$ for extension factor $s$, so angles stay in the trained range; short fine tuning recovers quality, but local resolution is compressed by $s$ for every frequency. NTK aware scaling: increase the base $b$ so low frequencies stretch most and high frequencies barely change. YaRN: interpolate per frequency band (no change for high frequency pairs whose wavelength is much shorter than the training length, full interpolation for the lowest), plus an attention temperature adjustment. Base increase at training time: Llama 3 uses $\theta = 500{,}000$; with $d_{\text{head}} = 128$ the slowest wavelength goes from about 54K tokens at base 10,000 to about 2.56M.
say: The problem is that positions past the training length produce rotation angles the model never saw. Position interpolation divides positions by the extension factor so everything maps back into the trained range, then you fine tune briefly; the downside is it also compresses local resolution for every frequency. NTK aware scaling instead raises the RoPE base, which stretches the slow frequencies a lot and the fast ones barely. YaRN makes that explicit per frequency band: leave high frequency pairs, which encode local order, alone, interpolate the low frequency ones, and adjust attention temperature. Llama 3 simply trained with a base of 500,000.
must_mention: unseen rotation angles past training length
interpolation divides positions by the factor

followups.q: Why keep the high frequency pairs unchanged?
followups.a: They encode fine local order, which interpolation would blur.

q: What are sliding window attention and attention sinks?
plain: Sliding window attention lets each token look only at the last W tokens instead of the whole history. For example, W might be the most recent 4,096 tokens. A window caps both the attention work and the cache size per layer. Stacking layers still lets information travel further back, step by step. Attention sinks are a few tokens at the very start of the sequence that models learn to dump spare attention onto. Keeping those first tokens in the cache, along with the recent window, keeps quality stable. Keeping sinks matters when old tokens are evicted (removed) during very long generation.
deep: Sliding window: mask $j < i - W$; per layer cost $O(TW)$, cache bounded at $W$ tokens with a rolling buffer; receptive field grows to about $L\times W$ across layers. Mistral 7B's config sets `sliding_window` to 4096. Many 2024 to 2026 models interleave local (windowed) and global layers to cut cache cost while keeping some full attention. Attention sinks (Xiao et al. 2023, StreamingLLM): softmax must place mass somewhere, and models put large weight on initial tokens; evicting them breaks generation, while keeping a handful of initial tokens plus a recent window allows streaming over very long inputs.
say: Sliding window attention restricts each token to the most recent W tokens, Mistral 7B uses 4,096, so per layer compute is linear in length and the cache can be a fixed size rolling buffer. Information can still flow further than W because each layer extends the reach, roughly layers times window. Many recent models mix windowed layers with a few global ones. Attention sinks are the observation that models park a lot of attention on the first few tokens, because softmax has to put mass somewhere. If you evict those during streaming, quality collapses, so streaming methods keep the first few tokens plus a recent window.
must_mention: attend only to the last W tokens

followups.q: What is Mistral 7B's window?
followups.a: 4,096 tokens, per its config.

q: How would you extend a model trained at 8K context to 128K?
plain: Extending a model from 8K to 128K tokens takes a multi step training recipe, not just a setting. First, change the position encoding so long distances map onto angles the model can handle. To do that, raise the base of RoPE (rotary position embedding) or use interpolation such as YaRN (yet another RoPE extension). Then continue pretraining (the first big round of training on lots of text) on genuinely long documents, growing the length in stages. Llama 3 went from 8K to 128K in six stages over about 800 billion tokens. Make the systems side fit, using FlashAttention and splitting long sequences across graphics processing units (GPUs). Then test on more than single fact retrieval, including whether short context quality slipped.
deep: **Positions:** raise the RoPE base (Llama 3: 500,000) or position interpolation, NTK aware scaling, YaRN. **Data and schedule:** continued pretraining on long documents, length increased in stages (Llama 3: six stages, about 800B tokens), document masking so packed documents do not attend to each other, keep a share of short data to avoid regressions. **Systems:** FlashAttention for linear memory, context parallelism (Llama 3 used CP 16 at 131,072 tokens), activation checkpointing; for serving, GQA and KV quantisation (Llama 3 8B: 16 GiB cache at 128K). **Evaluation:** needle tests are necessary not sufficient; multi fact retrieval, long document QA, and short context benchmarks for regressions.
say: I'd treat it as a training recipe, not just a config change. First the positions: raise the RoPE base or use interpolation like YaRN, which stretches the low frequencies while keeping the high frequency pairs that encode local order. Then continued pretraining on genuinely long documents, growing the length in stages; Llama 3 did eight to 128 thousand in six stages over roughly 800 billion tokens. On the systems side, FlashAttention, context parallelism, and a plan for the KV cache, which is 16 gigabytes per sequence for an 8B model at 128K. Finally evaluate beyond needle tests and check short context quality.
must_mention: staged continued pretraining on long data

followups.q: Why not just change max_position_embeddings?
followups.a: The model has never seen those positions or angles, so quality collapses past the trained length.

traps: Assuming a bigger window means the model uses it well.

q: What is a mixture of experts model?
plain: A mixture of experts (MoE) layer replaces the single feed forward network in each block with several expert networks. A small router (the part that picks experts) decides which networks each token uses. For every token, the router picks a few experts, often 2 out of 8. The layer's output is the picked experts' results combined using the router's weights. Think of a hospital where each patient sees two specialists rather than the whole staff. Attention and the embeddings stay shared. Only the feed forward part is split into experts.
deep: $\hat y = \sum_{i\in\operatorname{top}k(G(x))}G(x)_iE_i(x)$, gate $G$ from a linear router plus softmax (CME295 cheatsheet: an MoE activates only a portion of its neurons, routing each token to a subset of experts). Experts are usually SwiGLU FFNs; attention, norms and embeddings are dense. Sparse MoE decouples capacity (total parameters) from per token compute (active parameters). CME295 Lecture 3 covers dense versus sparse MoE and MoE in LLMs.
say: A mixture of experts layer replaces the one feed forward network in each block with several expert networks plus a small router. For each token, the router scores the experts, picks the top k, often two, and combines their outputs weighted by its scores. Attention and embeddings are still shared. The point is to decouple capacity from compute: the model has many more parameters overall, but each token only runs through a couple of experts, so per token FLOPs stay close to a much smaller dense model.
must_mention: router picks top k per token

followups.q: Which part of the block becomes the experts?
followups.a: The feed forward network.

source.title: Let's Data Science, 50 LLM and AI engineer interview questions for 2026

q: Why do total and active parameters differ in MoE? Work it out for Mixtral 8x7B.
plain: In a mixture of experts (MoE) model, total parameters count every expert, while active parameters count only the ones a token uses. All experts must be stored in memory, but each token only runs through the few the router picks. Mixtral 8x7B has 8 experts per layer and sends each token to 2. Counting from its published configuration, Mixtral has 46.7 billion parameters in total. But only 12.9 billion are used for any one token. So Mixtral computes like a 13 billion parameter model while needing memory for 47 billion. The total is not 56 billion (8 times 7) because the attention parts are shared.
deep: Mixtral config: 32 layers, $d = 4096$, 8 experts of SwiGLU hidden 14,336, top 2, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, $V = 32{,}000$, untied. Per expert per layer: $3\times4096\times14336 = 176.2$M. Attention 41.9M, router $4096\times8$, norms. Total: $32\times(41.9 + 8\times176.2 + \dots)$M + 262M embeddings $= 46.70$B. Active: $32\times(41.9 + 2\times176.2 + \dots)$M + 262M $= 12.88$B. Memory scales with total; FLOPs per token with active; weight bytes read per decode step depend on how many distinct experts the batch touches.
say: Every expert has to sit in memory, but each token only goes through the top k of them. Mixtral 8x7B, from its config, has 32 layers with 8 SwiGLU experts each, about 176 million parameters per expert per layer, and routes each token to two. Adding attention, the router and embeddings, that's 46.7 billion parameters in total, but only about 12.9 billion active per token. It isn't 56 billion because only the feed forward networks are replicated. So it computes like a 13B dense model but needs memory, and weight bandwidth at large batch, for 47B.
must_mention: only top k run per token

followups.q: Why does a large batch read most of the weights anyway?
followups.a: Different tokens pick different experts, so a big batch touches nearly all of them each step.

traps: Saying MoE reduces memory requirements.

source.title: Let's Data Science, 50 LLM and AI engineer interview questions for 2026

q: How does MoE routing work, and why does it tend to collapse?
plain: The router is a small linear layer that gives each expert a score for the current token. A softmax (a function that turns scores into weights) converts the scores into weights. The top two experts are kept, and their weights are rescaled to sum to one. Routing tends to collapse because early in training some experts happen to get more tokens. Those experts improve faster, so the router sends them even more tokens. Left alone, a few experts end up doing all the work while the others barely train. With experts spread over graphics processing units (GPUs), the busy ones also become bottlenecks. Busy experts may also have to drop tokens that exceed their capacity.
deep: Router: logits $W_rx$, softmax, top $k$, renormalise selected gates. Collapse: rich get richer dynamics between gate probabilities and expert quality. Systems effects: with expert parallelism, overloaded experts are stragglers; with a fixed expert capacity (capacity factor times average load), overflow tokens are dropped and pass through the residual only. Remedies: auxiliary load balancing loss, router z loss for stability, noise in routing during training, capacity limits, and bias based balancing (DeepSeek-V3).
say: The router is just a linear layer producing a score per expert for each token; you softmax, keep the top k, and renormalise those gate weights. The problem is a feedback loop: experts that get more tokens early get better, so the router sends them even more, and the rest starve, which wastes most of the model's capacity. On real hardware it's worse, because experts live on different GPUs, so a popular expert becomes a straggler, and with fixed capacity its overflow tokens get dropped. That's why MoE training always adds some balancing mechanism.

followups.q: What happens to a dropped token?
followups.a: It skips the expert computation for that layer and passes through on the residual connection.

q: Write the Switch Transformer load balancing loss and explain why it works.
plain: The Switch Transformer load balancing loss is a penalty that grows when the router sends too many tokens to a few experts. For each expert, multiply the fraction of tokens it actually received by the average probability the router gave it. Add these products over all experts. Then multiply by the number of experts and a small coefficient. If routing is perfectly even, the result is the coefficient times 1. If every token goes to one expert, it is the coefficient times the number of experts, which is 8 for 8 experts. Adding this penalty to the training loss pushes the router to spread tokens out. Mixtral's configuration sets the coefficient to 0.02.
deep:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{aux}} = \alpha\,E\sum_{i=1}^{E}f_iP_i,\quad f_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_t\mathbb{1}[\arg\max p_t = i],\quad P_i = \frac{1}{T}\sum_tp_{t,i}$$
$f_i$ is not differentiable but $P_i$ is, so gradients flow through $P_i$, lowering probability for overloaded experts. Minimised at $f_i = P_i = 1/E$, giving $\alpha$. Simulation with 8 experts, 512 tokens, random router: $E\sum f_iP_i = 1.007$; full collapse: 8.0. Mixtral's Hugging Face config: `router_aux_loss_coef` 0.02. DeepSeek-V3 (late 2024) instead adds per expert bias terms to routing scores, adjusted up or down by load, avoiding an auxiliary loss that can hurt quality.
say: The Switch Transformer loss is alpha times the number of experts times the sum over experts of f i times P i, where f i is the fraction of tokens dispatched to expert i and P i is the average router probability for expert i across the batch. With uniform routing both are one over E, so the sum times E is one. If everything goes to one expert it's E. The fraction f isn't differentiable, but P is, so the gradient pushes probability away from overloaded experts. Mixtral's config uses a coefficient of 0.02. DeepSeek-V3 replaced this with per expert bias adjustments.
must_mention: alpha times E times sum of f_i P_i
f_i is fraction of tokens routed

followups.q: Why not just penalise f_i directly?
followups.a: It comes from an argmax, so it has no gradient; P_i provides the differentiable path.

q: When is MoE a good choice, and what newer designs changed it?
plain: A mixture of experts (MoE) model is a good choice when you want more capacity without paying more compute per token. You also need enough total memory across graphics processing units (GPUs) to hold every expert. MoE is a poor fit for a single small GPU or a laptop, where memory is the limit. All experts must still be loaded, even though only a few are used per token. MoE also adds communication between GPUs and training instability. DeepSeek's designs split experts into many small ones plus a few always used shared experts. DeepSeek-V3, in late 2024, balanced load without an extra loss term (a penalty added to the training error).
deep: Good: compute bound training and high throughput serving across many GPUs, where FLOPs per token matter and memory is pooled. Bad: memory bound single device deployment; small batch decode still reads the chosen experts' weights, and large batches touch most experts. Costs: all to all communication under expert parallelism, load imbalance, routing instability, harder fine tuning. Designs: fine grained experts (many small experts, higher top $k$) plus shared experts that every token uses (DeepSeek MoE); auxiliary loss free balancing via adjustable per expert biases (DeepSeek-V3, December 2024). The CME295 cheatsheet lists expert parallelism among the main forms of parallelism.
say: MoE is a good trade when you're compute bound and memory is plentiful: large scale training or high throughput serving across many GPUs, where you get the quality of a much bigger model for the FLOPs of a smaller one. It's a bad fit when memory is the constraint, like a single consumer GPU, because every expert still has to be loaded. It also brings all to all communication, load balancing headaches and some instability. Newer designs from DeepSeek use many small fine grained experts plus a few shared experts every token passes through, and DeepSeek-V3 balanced load by adjusting per expert biases instead of an auxiliary loss.
must_mention: bad for memory bound single GPU
fine grained and shared experts, bias balancing

followups.q: What is a shared expert?
followups.a: An expert that every token passes through in addition to its routed experts, capturing common knowledge.

q: What is in context learning, and how is few shot prompting related?
plain: In context learning means a model picks up a task just from instructions or examples placed in its prompt. The model's weights do not change. Few shot prompting is the classic form of it. For example, show three English to French pairs, then a fourth English sentence. The model continues the pattern by translating the fourth sentence. Zero shot means instructions only, and one shot means a single example. The model is still only predicting the next token, and the examples tell it what kind of text it is continuing.
deep: Popularised by GPT-3 (Brown et al. 2020) with zero, one and few shot evaluation. Mechanistically nothing is learned in the weights; the forward pass conditions on the demonstrations. Ability grows with scale and with pretraining data that contains repeated formats. Practical levers: number of examples, ordering, format consistency, label balance, and selecting examples similar to the query (retrieval based few shot). CME295 Lecture 3 covers prompting strategies and in context learning; CS229 Lecture 14 covers transformers and in context learning.
say: In context learning is when a pretrained model performs a task just from what's in the prompt, instructions or examples, without any gradient update. Few shot prompting is the classic case: you show three or four input output pairs and the model continues the pattern on a new input. Zero shot is instructions only. The model is still just predicting the next token; the examples tell it what kind of document it's in and what format to follow. It's what made GPT-3 notable, and it's the reason a single pretrained model can do so many tasks without fine tuning.
must_mention: task from prompt, no weight update

followups.q: How would you choose few shot examples?
followups.a: Pick examples similar to the query, keep formats consistent, balance labels, and vary order to test sensitivity.

q: What are the leading explanations for how in context learning works?
plain: Researchers have three leading explanations, and they fit together rather than compete. One is implicit Bayesian inference (updating beliefs as evidence arrives). Documents in the pretraining data (the text the model first learns from) each have a hidden topic or task. Examples in the prompt are clues that let the model infer which task this document is doing. A second explanation, from studying model internals, is induction heads. Induction heads are pairs of attention heads that find an earlier spot where the current token appeared and copy what came next. A third explanation shows that transformers can carry out simple learning procedures inside a single forward pass. One example is steps of gradient descent (the standard way of training) on a regression problem (fitting a line to data).
deep: Implicit Bayesian inference (Xie et al. 2021, with Tengyu Ma, who teaches CS229 with Chris Ré): pretraining on documents with latent concepts makes the model approximately compute $p(\text{output}\mid\text{prompt}) = \int p(\text{output}\mid\theta)\,p(\theta\mid\text{prompt})\,d\theta$. Induction heads (Olsson et al. 2022): a previous token head plus a copying head implement $[A][B]\dots[A]\to[B]$; their formation during training coincides with a jump in in context learning. Learning algorithms in the forward pass (Garg et al. 2022; von Oswald et al. 2022): transformers trained on linear regression prompts match least squares and implement updates resembling gradient descent. CS229 Lecture 14 covers transformers and in context learning.
say: There are three complementary stories. The Bayesian one, from Xie and colleagues including Tengyu Ma, says pretraining documents have latent concepts, and the examples in the prompt are evidence about which concept generated this document, so the model effectively infers the task and predicts accordingly. The mechanistic one is induction heads: a pair of attention heads that find the previous occurrence of the current token and copy what followed, which supports pattern completion. And the algorithmic one shows transformers trained on regression prompts implement something like least squares or gradient descent steps inside the forward pass.
must_mention: implicit Bayesian inference over latent concepts

followups.q: What is an induction head?
followups.a: An attention head pair that finds an earlier occurrence of the current token and predicts the token that followed it.

q: How sensitive is few shot prompting to the examples, and what does that tell you?
plain: Few shot results can swing a lot with the order of the examples, their formatting, and how balanced their labels (the answers shown) are. Min and colleagues found in 2022 that replacing the correct labels in the examples with random ones often hurt much less than expected. The result suggests models lean heavily on the format and on the set of possible answers shown. Models do not rely only on whether each example is correct. In practice, keep formats consistent and balance the labels. Also check results across several orderings before trusting a number.
deep: Sensitivities: example order (recency effects), format and delimiters, label balance (majority label bias), and the label space shown. Min et al. (2022, "Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations"): random labels in demonstrations often degrade accuracy only modestly; the input distribution, label space and format matter more. Implications: report few shot results averaged over orderings and seeds; calibrate outputs; prefer retrieval of similar examples; for production, instructions plus a few well formatted examples are more stable than many examples.
say: It's surprisingly sensitive. Reordering the same examples, changing delimiters, or unbalancing the labels can move accuracy a lot, and models tend to favour labels that appear more often or more recently. Min and colleagues found that even randomising the labels in the demonstrations often hurt less than you'd expect, which suggests the model is mostly reading the format, the input distribution and the label space from the examples, not learning the mapping from each one. So I'd average results over several orderings, keep formats consistent, balance labels, and treat a single few shot number with suspicion.
must_mention: order, format and label balance matter
format and label space carry the signal

followups.q: What does that imply for evaluation?
followups.a: Report few shot results averaged over example orderings and seeds.

q: Are emergent abilities in LLMs real?
plain: Partly: the underlying loss (the training error) improves smoothly, but some task scores look sudden, partly because of how they are measured. Some benchmark scores seem to jump suddenly once models pass a certain size. Wei and colleagues called these jumps emergent abilities in 2022. Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo argued in 2023 that much of the jump comes from all or nothing scoring. If a model must get every token of an answer right, steady improvement per token looks like a sudden leap. Scoring the same outputs with partial credit shows smooth improvement.
deep: Wei et al. (2022): abilities near chance for small models and well above chance for large ones. Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo (2023): for fixed outputs, nonlinear or discontinuous metrics create apparent emergence, and continuous metrics show smooth, predictable gains; tested on the InstructGPT and GPT-3 family and a BIG-Bench meta analysis, and they induce apparent emergence in vision models by metric choice. Intuition: with per token accuracy $p$, exact match on an $L$ token answer scales like $p^L$, which looks like a threshold. Caveats: users care about the discontinuous metric, and some capabilities may still have real thresholds, but smooth loss scaling is what makes forecasting possible.
say: My view is that it's partly a measurement artefact. Wei and colleagues documented tasks where small models are at chance and large models suddenly succeed. Schaeffer and colleagues showed that if you hold model outputs fixed and switch from an all or nothing metric like exact match to a continuous one, the curves become smooth. The intuition is that if per token accuracy improves gradually, getting a ten token answer exactly right scales like that accuracy to the tenth power, which looks like a sudden jump. That doesn't mean nothing changes with scale, and users care about exact correctness, but loss scales smoothly.
must_mention: per token accuracy to the power L

followups.q: Why does this matter for planning?
followups.a: If gains are smooth under continuous metrics, capabilities can be forecast from smaller models.

traps: Claiming emergence is either fully real or fully fake.

q: Why do LLMs hallucinate, at the level of the model itself?
plain: Hallucination, which means stating false things fluently, happens because the model is trained to produce text that looks likely, not text that is true. A false sentence written in the style of a true one can look just as likely. Facts seen only once or twice in training, such as an obscure person's birthday, are hard to tell apart from plausible made up values. Once the model writes one wrong token, it tends to stay consistent with it. Sampling (picking a token at random by its probability) at high temperature (more randomness) reaches for unlikely tokens. The model's knowledge also stops at its training cutoff (the date its data ended).
deep: Causes: (1) likelihood objective rewards plausibility; (2) statistical pressure: Kalai et al. (2025) frame generation errors through binary classification, so if valid and invalid statements cannot be separated from data, pretraining yields some invalid ones, and rarely seen facts are most exposed; (3) evaluation and post training reward guessing over abstaining; (4) exposure bias and snowballing on its own outputs; (5) decoding from the tail (high temperature, wide top p); (6) knowledge limits: data cutoff, lossy compression of the corpus into fixed weights, contradictory sources.
say: At the model level I'd give a few causes. First, the objective: next token prediction rewards text that looks like the training data, and a false statement written like a true one gets high probability. Second, rare facts: something seen once in training, like an obscure person's birthday, can't be distinguished from a plausible made up value. Third, the model conditions on its own output, so one wrong token snowballs. Fourth, sampling at high temperature reaches into the unreliable tail. And a 2025 OpenAI paper adds incentives: benchmarks give no credit for saying I don't know, so training rewards confident guessing.

followups.q: Will more pretraining data fix it?
followups.a: It helps common facts but does little for facts seen once, so no.

traps: Saying more data will eliminate hallucination.

source.title: techinterview.org, What LLM interviewers actually ask about transformers

q: Why does hallucination persist after post training, according to Kalai et al. 2025?
plain: Hallucination persists because most benchmarks (standard tests) reward guessing over saying "I don't know". Most benchmarks grade an answer as simply right or wrong, and give nothing for "I don't know". Under right or wrong scoring, guessing always scores at least as well as admitting uncertainty. Guessing here is like guessing on a multiple choice exam with no penalty for wrong answers. Post training (extra training after the first big round, called pretraining) optimises for those scores, so models learn to bluff confidently. The authors propose changing how existing benchmarks are scored. Then abstaining (declining to answer) would not be penalised relative to confident errors.
deep: Kalai, Nachum, Vempala and Zhang, "Why Language Models Hallucinate" (September 2025): pretraining errors share the statistics of binary classification errors; after post training, hallucinations persist because evaluations are mostly binary and reward guessing, so models become good test takers. Proposed fix (socio technical): modify the scoring of mainstream leaderboards, for example penalising confident errors more than abstentions or stating an explicit confidence threshold, rather than adding separate hallucination evals. Practical implication: measure abstention and calibration alongside accuracy.
say: Their argument is about incentives. Almost every benchmark scores an answer as right or wrong, with zero for abstaining, so from the model's point of view a guess has positive expected score and saying I don't know has none. Post training optimises for those scores, so models learn to bluff like a student on a multiple choice exam with no penalty for wrong answers. Their proposed fix isn't another hallucination benchmark, it's changing the scoring of existing mainstream ones so confident errors cost more than abstentions. For my own evals that means tracking abstention and calibration, not just accuracy.

followups.q: What does this imply for building an eval?
followups.a: Score abstentions separately and penalise confident wrong answers.

q: How would you detect and reduce hallucinations at the model level?
plain: To detect hallucinations without ground truth (a known correct answer), ask the same question several times with sampling (random picking). If the answers disagree, the model probably does not know. You can also check the probabilities the model gives its own answer tokens. Low or spread out probabilities signal uncertainty. To reduce hallucinations, give the model sources to quote from, which is called retrieval. Also lower the temperature (the randomness setting) for factual questions. And train or prompt the model to say when it is unsure. For example, a bot asked for a citation should be given the document and asked to quote it, not to recall it.
deep: Detection: self consistency across samples (disagreement signals ignorance), token level log probabilities and entropy, claim level checking against retrieved passages (techinterview.org suggests scoring each claim against sources). Reduction at the model and decoding level: grounding via retrieval with citations (RAG module), low temperature or greedy for factual tasks, calibrated abstention trained in post training, rewarding "I don't know" in evals (Kalai et al. 2025), constrained decoding to force answers to quote provided spans. Prompt design: instruct the model to answer only from given context and to say when the answer is absent.
say: For detection without labels, my first tool is self consistency: sample the answer several times, and if the samples disagree on the key facts, the model likely doesn't know. Token log probabilities and entropy on the answer give a cheaper, rougher signal, and with sources available you can check each claim against retrieved passages. To reduce hallucination, I ground the model with retrieval and citations, lower temperature for factual tasks, and prompt or train it to abstain when evidence is missing. And on the evaluation side, I'd reward abstention, since benchmarks that don't are part of why models guess.

followups.q: Why does sampling disagreement signal hallucination?
followups.a: Known facts get consistent high probability; fabricated details vary from sample to sample.

topic: Prefill, decode and the KV cache
q: Walk me through what happens from the moment a prompt arrives to the first generated token.
plain: The prompt becomes a vector per token, runs through every block once, and the last position's output picks the first token. First, the text is tokenised into ids, and each id is looked up in the embedding table (one vector per token) to get a vector. All prompt tokens then pass through every block in one parallel prefill pass (reading the whole prompt at once). Each block normalises (rescales the numbers) and runs attention with the causal mask (which hides later tokens) and positions applied. The block then adds the result back, normalises again, runs the feed forward network (a small network per token), and adds back again. While the blocks run, each layer's keys and values are saved in the cache. After the final normalisation, only the last position's vector is multiplied by the output matrix, which gives a score for every vocabulary token. A decoding rule such as temperature plus top p picks the first token, which is decoded to text and streamed back.
deep: 1. Tokenise (byte level BPE, special tokens from the chat template). 2. Embed: $E[\text{ids}]$ (plus learned positions in GPT-2; RoPE models rotate q and k inside attention). 3. Prefill: for each of $L$ blocks, $x\leftarrow x + \operatorname{Attn}(\operatorname{Norm}(x))$, $x\leftarrow x + \operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{Norm}(x))$, writing $K, V$ per layer to the (paged) cache; compute bound, uses FlashAttention. 4. Final norm, logits $h_TW_U$ for the last position only. 5. Decoding: temperature, top p or min p, optional grammar mask, sample. 6. Detokenise and stream. Time to first token is dominated by step 3; every later token repeats steps 3 to 6 for one position, reading weights and the cache (memory bound).
say: The prompt, wrapped in the chat template, is tokenised into ids with byte level BPE. Each id is looked up in the embedding table. Then prefill: all the prompt tokens go through every block in one parallel pass, normalise, attention with the causal mask and RoPE applied to queries and keys, residual add, normalise, feed forward, residual add, and each layer writes its keys and values into the cache. After the final norm, only the last position goes through the output projection to get logits. The sampler applies temperature and top p, picks a token, and it's detokenised and streamed. After that, decode repeats this one token at a time.
must_mention: write keys and values to the cache
logits for the last position only

followups.q: Which step dominates time to first token?
followups.a: Prefill, which is compute bound and scales with prompt length.

q: How would you make inference for a 70B model faster and cheaper?
plain: Start with memory, because decoding is limited by the number of bytes read. Quantise the weights (store them with fewer bits) to 8 or 4 bits. Quantising shrinks 141 gigabytes (GB) of 16 bit weights to about 35 GB at 4 bits and speeds up each token. Use a serving engine with continuous batching and paged KV (key value) memory so the graphics processing unit (GPU) always has a full batch. Use FlashAttention for long prompts. Then add speculative decoding for lower latency (response time) at small batch sizes. Add prefix caching (reusing the cache for a shared start of prompts) for shared system prompts. Split the model across GPUs with tensor parallelism (splitting each weight matrix across GPUs) if it does not fit on one.
deep: Levers by bottleneck: **weights** (memory bound decode): int8, int4 (GPTQ, AWQ) or FP8; 70.6B in bf16 is about 141 GB, int4 about 35 GB. **KV cache:** GQA is built in (Llama 3 70B has 8 KV heads, 320 KiB per token), KV int8 or fp8, PagedAttention, prefix caching. **Utilisation:** continuous batching, chunked prefill, right sized batch for latency targets. **Latency:** speculative decoding (draft, Medusa, EAGLE) at small batch. **Kernels:** FlashAttention, fused kernels, CUDA graphs. **Parallelism:** tensor parallelism inside a node (the techinterview.org guide asks how to serve 70B on 4 A100 80GB and how to choose TP=2 versus TP=4). **Model choice:** a smaller or distilled model, or MoE, if quality allows. Measure TTFT, TPOT and throughput before and after each change.
say: I'd start from the bottleneck, which for decode is memory bandwidth. First, quantise weights: a 70B model is about 140 gigabytes in bf16, around 35 at four bits with AWQ or GPTQ, which both fits on fewer GPUs and cuts bytes read per token. Second, use an engine like vLLM for continuous batching and paged KV cache, plus prefix caching for shared system prompts and KV quantisation for long contexts. Third, tensor parallelism across GPUs in a node for capacity and bandwidth. For latency at small batch, add speculative decoding. And I'd measure time to first token, time per token and throughput after each change.
must_mention: quantise weights to int8 or int4

followups.q: Would you use tensor parallelism of 2 or 4?
followups.a: The smallest degree that fits weights plus the needed cache with headroom; more GPUs add bandwidth but also communication.

q: You have a fixed training compute budget. How do you decide model size and number of tokens?
plain: Start from the Chinchilla rule as a baseline, then adjust for how the model will be used. For the best model at a given training cost, use about 20 tokens per parameter, which splits the compute evenly between size and data. Compute is 6 times the parameters times the tokens. For example, a budget of about 5.88 times 10 to the 23 operations gives about 70 billion parameters on 1.4 trillion tokens. Next, if the model will serve heavy traffic after training, pick a smaller model and train it on many more tokens. The reason is that every generated token costs compute in proportion to model size. Check that you actually have that much good, deduplicated data, since repeating data has diminishing value. Finally, fit your own small scale curves on your data and tokeniser instead of trusting published constants.
deep: Baseline: $C = 6ND$ with $D\approx20N$ gives $N\approx\sqrt{C/120}$; for $C = 5.88\text{e}23$ that is about 70B on 1.4T tokens (Chinchilla). Inference aware: minimise $6ND + 2N\cdot D_{\text{served}}$; heavy traffic pushes toward Llama 3 8B style training at about 1,900 tokens per parameter. Data constraint: unique high quality tokens may cap $D$; a few epochs of repetition cost little, many cost a lot. Calibrate: IsoFLOP sweeps on small models with your tokeniser and data (Llama 3's own fit chose 402B on 16.55T for 3.8e25). Schedule: match the cosine cycle to the planned length (Chinchilla's 25 percent overshoot warning).
say: I'd anchor on Chinchilla: with compute equal to six N D and about 20 tokens per parameter, the compute optimal model size is roughly the square root of the budget over 120, which gives Chinchilla's 70 billion on 1.4 trillion tokens at its budget. Then I'd adjust for inference: if the model will serve a lot of traffic, I'd pick a smaller model and train it far longer, the Llama 3 8B approach. I'd check data availability, since I need that many good unique tokens. And I'd run my own small IsoFLOP sweeps on my data and tokeniser, and make sure the learning rate schedule matches the planned length.
must_mention: Chinchilla baseline about 20 tokens per parameter

followups.q: What model size does the 20 tokens rule give for 5.9e23 FLOPs?
followups.a: About 70B parameters on 1.4T tokens, Chinchilla itself.
